proposed_edges.relationship: History as “the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies”: national myths, anachronism and schoolbook pasts that historians must resist “as they are being formed” (1993 lecture)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, read in full ("The New Threat to History", lecture opening the academic year at the Central European University, published in the NYRB, 16 December 1993; no pagination). "For history is the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies, as poppies are the raw material for heroin addiction … If there is no suitable past, it can always be invented"; "The most usual ideological abuse of history is based on anachronism rather than lies" (examples: Macedonia, Croatian schoolbooks, Ayodhya, Kosovo 1389); "History is not ancestral memory or collective tradition. It is what people learned from priests, schoolmasters, the writers of history books"; "We must resist the formation of national, ethnic, and other myths, as they are being formed." He also credits criticism of national myths "from within" (Israel, Ireland). The link to The Invention of Tradition (1983) rests only on the lecture's own "it can always be invented" and the existing publisher record; the 1983 introduction is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Age of… volumes (1962–1994) as a synthesis of “the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991”, praised by reviewers for range and analytical grasp and called “unashamedly Eurocentric” by Judt
proposed_edges.map_label: The Age of… synthesis, 1962–94, per reviewers
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the four volumes are unread. Guardian obituarists (2012, read in full): the series "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy". Judt (NYRB 1995, read in full): the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation, now exposed to steady criticism and revision"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (his endnote 2 defends the European focus). Black (Historein 2003–4, p. 215): "authoritative and commanding overviews of international history from the 18th century to present". Anderson (LRB 2002) quotes Hobsbawm on Interesting Times as "world history shaping that experience". At the 2014 conference (Times Higher Education report) Mazower spoke of a "golden age of historical synthesis". Counterweights: Judt's Eurocentrism remark and the existing critiques by Guha and Chakrabarty (edges 979, 917).

proposed_edges.relationship: Tony Judt: The Age of Extremes keeps the categories of the 1930s, gives Bolshevism “no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms”, devotes “just six pages” to “real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia and neglects nationalism (1995)
proposed_edges.map_label: Judt on The Age of Extremes, 1995
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A named reader without a node, drawn from political history because his charge concerns the book's political history. Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Industrial Britain and its workers: the standard-of-living debate of the 1950s and Industry and Empire (1968), which his readers credit with recasting the economic history of Britain
proposed_edges.map_label: Standard of living and Industry and Empire, per readers
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated: no economic-history text by Hobsbawm was read (his 1957 Economic History Review article is metadata only). Judt (NYRB 1995): Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one at that". Guardian obituarists (2012): the "once celebrated 'standard of living' debate", in which he and R. M. Hartwell "traded arguments in successive numbers of the Economic History Review", and Industry and Empire (1968) as "a compelling summation of much of his work on Britain and the industrial revolution". Black (Historein, p. 215): "a key protagonist in the standard of living in the industrial revolution debates … something of a Cold War battleground". A pre-2000 gap repair; not a claim about the transition debate.

new_sources.title: Eric Hobsbawm, “The New Threat to History,” New York Review of Books, 16 December 1993 (lecture opening the academic year at the Central European University, Budapest).
new_sources.citation: Eric Hobsbawm, “The New Threat to History,” New York Review of Books, 16 December 1993 (lecture opening the academic year at the Central European University, Budapest).

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). Headnote: the lecture "was given at the beginning of the academic year at the Central European University"; he opens: "It is an honor to be asked to open this academic year" (delivered autumn 1993, exact day not given). "For history is the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies, as poppies are the raw material for heroin addiction … If there is no suitable past, it can always be invented." "I used to think that the profession of history, unlike that of, say, nuclear physics, could at least do no harm. Now I know it can." "We cannot invent our facts. Either Elvis Presley is dead or he isn’t", against "“postmodernist” intellectual fashions" (a brief passage: "I need say little about the first of these responsibilities"). "The most usual ideological abuse of history is based on anachronism rather than lies." "History is not ancestral memory or collective tradition. It is what people learned from priests, schoolmasters, the writers of history books". "We must resist the formation of national, ethnic, and other myths, as they are being formed. It will not make us popular." Whether this is the On History chapter "Outside and Inside History" is not verified.

new_sources.title: Tony Judt, “Downhill All the Way,” New York Review of Books, 25 May 1995; review of Eric Hobsbawm, The Age of Extremes: A History of the World, 1914–1991 (Pantheon, 1994).
new_sources.citation: Tony Judt, “Downhill All the Way,” New York Review of Books, 25 May 1995; review of Eric Hobsbawm, The Age of Extremes: A History of the World, 1914–1991 (Pantheon, 1994).

verification.note: Complete text and endnotes read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). A "Hobsbawm generation" of historians who began between about 1959 and 1975; Primitive Rebels "first appeared in 1959"; Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation"; The Age of Revolution 1962, The Age of Capital 1975 ("Hobsbawm’s single greatest work"), The Age of Empire twelve years later. Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one" who "mostly avoids military or political narrative"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (endnote 2 defends the European focus). The "one" defect: "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject". Verdict: "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.

new_sources.title: Perry Anderson, “The Age of EJH,” London Review of Books 24, no. 19 (3 October 2002); review of Eric Hobsbawm, Interesting Times: A Twentieth-Century Life (Allen Lane, 2002).
new_sources.citation: Perry Anderson, “The Age of EJH,” London Review of Books 24, no. 19 (3 October 2002); review of Eric Hobsbawm, Interesting Times: A Twentieth-Century Life (Allen Lane, 2002).

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147 (LRB page; no pagination). The memoir is offered as the "flip side" of Age of Extremes, "not world history illustrated by the experiences of an individual, but world history shaping that experience" (Hobsbawm as quoted); "a kind of fifth volume, in more personal register, of a continuous project". On remaining in the Party after 1956 (Hobsbawm quoted): "I still belong to the tail-end of the first generation of Communists"; Anderson: "Most people would see in it evidence of an exceptional integrity and strength of character". Criticism: "His treatment of the traditions of others is much less impressive. Here a lack of generosity disfigures too many judgments" (Samuel, Thompson, the New Lefts); no "real intellectual engagement with the issues that haunted the trajectory of European Communism"; Marxism Today's role in "preparing the cult of Thatcher". On history: Hobsbawm gives "a good account of the rise of the analytic social history associated with the Annales and Past & Present … regretting its later retreat with the cultural turn of the 1980s" (Anderson's report); his thinking about the past is more original than Braudel's, to be seen in On History (Anderson's judgment). The memoir is unread.

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147. new_sources.title: Terry Eagleton, “Indomitable,” London Review of Books 33, no. 5 (3 March 2011); review of Eric Hobsbawm, How to Change the World: Marx and Marxism 1840–2011 (Little, Brown, 2011).
new_sources.citation: Terry Eagleton, “Indomitable,” London Review of Books 33, no. 5 (3 March 2011); review of Eric Hobsbawm, How to Change the World: Marx and Marxism 1840–2011 (Little, Brown, 2011).

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147. Most pieces were published before, about two-thirds not in English, including "three substantial surveys of the history of Marxism from 1880 to 1983"; Hobsbawm "remains broadly committed to the Marxist camp – a fact worth mentioning as it would be easy to read this book without realising it. This is because of its judiciousness, not its shiftiness"; he "insists on Marx’s substantial debt" to the utopian socialists and "denies that it [the Manifesto] is a deterministic document". Criticism: "Like many historians he is not at his sharpest in the realm of ideas", wrong about how Louis Althusser's followers read Capital; feminism, "not least Marxist feminism", treated with "cold-eyed indifference" and Trotskyism consigned "to a few casual asides". In the same paragraph of criticisms: "Hobsbawm also thinks that Gramsci is the most original thinker produced by the West since 1917" (Eagleton's report, not his own judgment). The book is unread.

verification.note: Complete review read for revision 1.147. The book was published on 25 March 2013, after his death: "the posthumous publication of this stimulating collection" of about two dozen texts, several published for the first time; Hobsbawm quoted on "an era of history which has lost its bearings". Morgan's reservations: Hobsbawm's claim about the status of the arts before 1914 "is really enormous. It has to be tackled head on or quietly ignored. Hobsbawm chose the latter course"; on music he is "unfairly castigating concert programmes". A sidebar on the page misdates How to Change the World; not used. The book is unread.
